title: How to Lead a Prayer Meeting People Come To
subtitle: Reviving the church prayer meeting with structure, honesty, and expectancy so corporate prayer stops being the night everyone skips

sections.title: The Night Nobody Comes
sections.body:
In most churches the prayer meeting is the least attended gathering on the calendar, and we have made an uneasy peace with that. A handful of the faithful, a long list of physical ailments, a slow hour, and the quiet understanding that this is just how it is.

We say prayer is the engine of the church. Then we schedule it at the hour we are most willing to skip.

The empty prayer room is a sermon we are preaching without meaning to. It says, more loudly than any pulpit, that we believe in our own effort and not in our asking. The early church was born in a prayer meeting and sustained by them, and the great awakenings ran on them. We have not lost the doctrine of prayer. We have lost the practice, and then blamed the people for not coming to a meeting we ourselves did not expect God to show up to. The revival of the prayer meeting begins with that confession, and it has to begin with the pastor.

sections.title: Why the Meeting Died
sections.body:
The prayer meeting did not die because people stopped believing in prayer. It died because we made it boring, shapeless, and strangely impersonal.

It became a meeting about prayer instead of a meeting of prayer. We spent forty minutes discussing requests and ten minutes actually praying.

Think about the typical hour. A long recitation of medical updates about people no one in the room has met. A leader who does most of the talking. Little structure, so the bold pray and the quiet sit silent and ashamed. No sense that anything is actually expected to happen. Of course it emptied out. We took the most powerful privilege given to the church, direct access to the throne of God, and turned it into the dullest hour of the week. The problem was never prayer. The problem was what we did to it. And what we did to it, we can undo.

sections.title: Give the Hour Shape
sections.body:
Prayer in a group needs structure, not because the Spirit needs managing, but because people need help, and a shapeless hour helps no one.

Do not open the floor and hope. Lead it. Move the room through movements, the way Scripture itself teaches us to pray.

Begin with praise, with adoration, with God himself and not our needs, because a room that starts by beholding God prays differently than a room that starts with its problems. Move to confession, real and unhurried, because unconfessed sin sits like a stone in corporate prayer. Then thanksgiving, naming what God has already done. Then, finally, the requests, and shape these too, praying first for the lost and the kingdom before the aches and pains, lest the meeting collapse into a clinic. Pray Scripture out loud. Pray in shorter sentences so the timid can join. Break into pairs so no one hides. Structure is not the enemy of the Spirit. It is the trellis the Spirit grows on, the help that lets ordinary people pray with confidence instead of fear.

sections.title: Come Expecting God to Answer
sections.body:
The deepest difference between a dead prayer meeting and a living one is not the format. It is expectancy. One room is performing a duty. The other believes the God it is addressing actually hears and actually moves.

We will not draw people to a meeting we ourselves attend without hope. Expectancy is contagious, and so is its absence.

So teach the church what prayer is for, and then report back when God answers, because nothing fills a prayer room like a congregation that has watched its prayers come true. Keep the requests and revisit them. Tell the stories. Let the people see, again and again, that the asking was not into the void. The disciples in the upper room did not pray as a formality. They prayed as people waiting for something, and the something came. A church that prays like that is a church that has remembered who it is talking to. The hour stops being a chore and becomes the place people would not miss.

sections.title: It Starts on Your Own Knees
sections.body:
I will not pretend I have always led this well. There were seasons I prepared the sermon with great care and walked into the prayer meeting with nothing prepared at all, including my own heart.

A congregation will not pray more fervently than its pastor, and it can usually tell the difference between a man leading prayer and a man who actually prays.

The revival of the prayer meeting is not first a matter of technique. It is a matter of a leader who has been alone with God before he asks the people to gather. You cannot lead a room into a place you do not yourself live. So before you fix the format, fix your own knees. Let the congregation catch you praying, not performing prayer from a platform, but plainly desperate for God in front of them. That is what they will follow. Not a better structured hour, though structure helps. A man who clearly believes that when the church prays, heaven leans in. Build that, and they will come, because people are starving to pray with someone who means it.

furtherReading.title: The Hour That Changes the World
furtherReading.author: Dick Eastman
